result.summary: Pausanias describes the Achaian towns of Pharae and Tritea, including the oracle of Hermes of the Market-place, a grove of Castor and Pollux, a painted tomb and the founding legends of Tritea. He ends with the coastal route from Patrae to Aegium and two local rivers.

scenes.title: Pharae and its oracle
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes Pharae, its river, plane-trees, the market-place Hermes with its curious oracle, sacred well, square stones and the grove of Castor and Pollux.

scenes.title: Road to Tritea and its founding
scenes.summary: On the way to Tritea stands a tomb painted by Nicias. Pausanias gives two accounts of the town's founding and describes its temples and cults.

scenes.title: Coast road to Aegium
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists distances along the coast from Patrae to Aegium and mentions the rivers Milichus and Charadrus.

alias_notes.explanation: Cult title of the square statue at Pharae.

notable_quotes.reason: Climax of the unusual oracle ritual: the first words overheard are the answer.
Records that early Greeks worshipped unhewn stones rather than statues.

analysis.text: Pausanias records local cults, oracles and founding legends, showing how Greek towns tied identity to gods and heroes.
Mentions of towns joined to Patrae by Augustus and statues taken to Rome reflect Roman rule's effect on Achaia.

fun_facts.text: The Pharae oracle works by cledonomancy, interpreting the first chance words overheard as an answer.

language_notes.text: A stade was a Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet (about 180 metres), so 150 stades is around 17 miles.
Olenus was an ancient Achaian city, already in ruins in Pausanias' day. He mentions it to identify the river by a known landmark.
"The ordinary piece of money, a brass coin" means the standard local small coin, the fee for consulting the oracle.
The first words overheard by chance, after unstopping the ears, are taken as the god's answer. This kind of divination is called cledonomancy.
Apis was the sacred bull of Egypt, worshipped at Memphis. Pausanias compares the oracle to Egyptian practice.
"Unhewn stones" are rough, uncarved stones. Pausanias notes that early Greeks worshipped such stones instead of carved images.
"Reckoned with Patræ by Imperial order" means the Roman emperor made Tritea part of the territory of Patræ.
A stade was a Greek measure of about 600 feet (roughly 185 metres), so 120 stades is around 14 miles.
A sun-shade is a parasol, carried by attendants to shield a lady of rank.
Cumæ in the Opic land is the Greek colony in Campania, Italy; Opici was a Greek name for the early inhabitants there.
The Greatest Gods are a cult of uncertain identity. The festival comparison points to Dionysus's wine festivals, which were widespread.
"Sail along the coast" gives the sea distance; the land route to Ægium is 40 stades shorter.
Triclaria was a cult of Artemis at Patræ, linked to the story of Melanippus and Comaetho.

context_notes.text: Augustus, the first Roman emperor, reorganised Achaia after 31 BC and joined Pharæ to the territory of Patræ.
Hermes, god of messengers, travellers and trade, suits a market-place statue. Square, bearded pillar-like forms of him were common.
Castor and Pollux were twin sons of Leda, worshipped as protectors of sailors and horsemen.
Rome carried off many Greek statues as spoils or treasures, so such reports of removed statues were common.
Nicias of Athens was a famous painter of the later fourth century BC, so a tomb painted by him would be notable.
Ares is the Greek god of war. Triton is a sea god, and Athene's epithet Tritonis is linked to him.
Rome carried off many Greek statues as spoils or decoration, which Pausanias often records.
Rhium is the promontory at the mouth of the Gulf of Corinth, the narrowest point of the gulf.

literary_notes.text: The claim that a person can eat and sleep inside the trees stresses their huge age and size, though it may be literal.
The god's answer depends on pure chance, which gives the ritual an ironic mix of careful ceremony and randomness.
Pausanias openly admits the limits of his knowledge, showing the cautious, personal voice of a traveller-historian.
Pausanias openly admits his ignorance and reports only the common inference, showing the cautious, honest traveller-historian.
Two rival founding stories explain the town's name and origin, one human and one mythic, left side by side without judgment.
The aside on the river's effect on cattle adds local marvel and curiosity to a dry list of distances.
